message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for highly parallel, data‑intensive tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with powerful, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput; each core can execute the same instruction on many data elements simultaneously (SIMD). |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex, variable‑length instructions; supports a wide range of operations. | Often simpler, fixed‑length instructions; focuses on arithmetic and memory operations that can be parallelized. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth, low latency. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on massive shared memory and high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR). |
| **Execution Model** | Out‑of‑order execution, deep pipelines, branch prediction. | In‑order execution, wide SIMD lanes, massive thread blocks. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Sequential or lightly parallel tasks, branching code, I/O‑bound operations. | Data‑parallel tasks: matrix multiplication, convolution, image processing, simulations, deep‑learning inference/training. |
| **Power & Heat** | Designed for low power per core, efficient for single‑thread performance. | High throughput per watt for parallel workloads; can consume more power overall but is efficient when fully utilized. |
| **Programming** | C/C++, assembly, high‑level languages; single‑threaded performance matters. | CUDA/OpenCL, specialized libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN); focus on vectorized kernels and thread blocks. |

In short, a CPU excels at handling diverse, sequential tasks with complex control flow, while a GPU shines when you need to perform the same operation on many data items at once. That’s why modern systems often combine both: the CPU manages the overall system and orchestrates tasks, while the GPU accelerates compute‑heavy, parallel portions.
